title: Sugar
subtitle: 1200–300 BC · The Reed Reaches the Mainland: Hybrid Canes, the Vedic Cane, the Buddha’s Syrup and Honey Without Bees

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Atharvaveda’s cane, the sweet cane of the prophets, the Buddha’s syrup and the Ikṣvāku descent

entries.label: The Atharvaveda names the cane (ikṣu)
entries.hint: Sugarcane is absent from the Rigveda (c.1500 BC) and first recorded about 1000 BC in the Atharvaveda, composed when Sanskrit-speaking peoples had spread from the north-west to Bengal. The verse may therefore record a cultigen already present in pre-Aryan Bengal rather than the date of its introduction. Popular accounts speak of verses on a cane bow and a cane-circle charm, which were not checked in the Sanskrit.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Needham, Science and Civilisation in China 6.3 (Daniels & Menzies 1996) p.134 n.b, citing Daniels & Daniels, ‘Sugarcane in Prehistory’, Archaeology in Oceania 28(1) (1993) p.7; Hutchinson (3): sugarcane is not recorded at Indian archaeological sites although wild S. spontaneum is (Vishnu-Mittre (1) p.26); Chaitanya (1) p.33 for the Aryan expansion to Bengal. The cane-bow and cane-circle descriptions come from reading-passage pages drawing on a popular book and are unverified; verse numbers not located.

entries.label: The prophets’ ‘sweet cane from a far country’
entries.hint: Jeremiah (6:20) scorns incense from Sheba and ‘the sweet cane from a far country’, and Isaiah (43:24) says ‘thou hast bought me no sweet cane with money’. A Hebrew word for a fragrant imported reed, qaneh, is sometimes read as sugarcane, but most reference works identify an aromatic grass such as calamus or Cymbopogon, whose sweetness is of scent, not taste.
entries.note: CONTESTED (reference works): Needham SCC 6.3 p.145 (the passage in which ‘the sweet cane of the Old Testament was kaneh’ is set among words that ‘could have formed an international patois for sugarcane along the Silk Road’ — speculative); the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia ‘Reed’, a calamus entry and the hypr.bible lexicon list Cymbopogon, Indian grasses (Zohary and Moldenke favour ginger-grass) and Acorus calamus as the candidates, with the sweetness of scent. Not evidence for sugarcane.

entries.label: The Pātimokkha allows syrup to sick monks
entries.hint: The Pātimokkha, the monks’ rule codified in the Buddha’s own lifetime or that of his disciples, already allows syrup (phāṇita) to the sick as one of the five medicines — on Daniels’s chronology the first cane product in the record. Sugar’s first religious status is as medicine.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Pali not read): Needham SCC 6.3 p.367 and nn. (Daniels), citing Thomas (1) p.15 and Oldenberg (2) vol.1 p.xv for the codification c.−500, Oldenberg (2) vol.3 p.77 and Horner (1) vol.1 p.133 for phāṇita and the five medicines. Compare the later Vinaya redaction in sugar-300bc-600ad::b1. The dating of the Pātimokkha is Daniels’s and Thomas’s; Mazumdar (1998) n.63 dates the Vinaya Piṭaka to the 3rd century BC (after S. N. Sen).

entries.label: The Buddha ‘born of sugarcane’: the Ikṣvāku descent
entries.hint: Sugar and sugarcane are widely mentioned in Buddhist literature from about 500 BC, and the Buddha is later called ‘King of Sugarcane’ and ‘born of sugarcane’ because the Śākya clan traced its ancestry to the legendary Ikṣvāku (ikṣu means sugarcane), the son of Manu. The genealogy is tradition, but it shows the cane written into the founder’s lineage.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 pp.61 and 134 n.b (Daniels & Daniels (2) pp.36–38 for the Buddhist literature; Soothill & Hodous (1) p.195); Mazumdar (1998) pp.21–22; Kieschnick (2003) p.250. The epithet ‘King of Sugarcane’ is attested in Mahāyāna texts translated into Chinese, centuries after the Buddha; the genealogy itself was not traced to a Pali passage here.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Cane words in the Yue languages, the shift of śarkarā and Nearchus’s reeds

entries.label: Cane words in the Yue languages and archaic Chinese
entries.hint: The linguist Paul Benedict traced roots for ‘sugarcane’ in the Thai and Kadai languages of the Yue peoples of the south China coast, and their transfer into archaic Chinese about 1200 BC — evidence that cane was a Yue cultigen long before Han writers described it. The method has been criticised, but Needham judges that sugarcane was undoubtedly a Yue crop.
entries.note: CONTESTED: Needham SCC 6.3 p.134 n.c, citing Benedict (3) p.324, with the criticism of Bellwood (1) pp.38, 123 and Pulleyblank (1) p.436. The date c.1200 BC is Benedict’s estimate of the loan, not an attestation in a text.

entries.label: Śarkarā: from ‘gravel’ to sugar
entries.hint: The Sanskrit word śarkarā means gravel or sandy particles in the Vedic texts and later names granulated sugar — the word that travels west as sákchar, saccharum and ‘sugar’. When the shift happened is disputed: one scholar puts it after 500 BC, while Needham finds śarkarā emerging in the Arthaśāstra and the medical texts, centuries later.
entries.note: CONTESTED DATE: Mazumdar (1998) n.32 (Monier-Williams: ‘granulated sugar after 500 B.C. but meaning gravel or sandy particles earlier in Vedic texts’); against Needham SCC 6.3 p.368 (śarkarā emerging in the Arthaśāstra, mean date 100 BC, and the Caraka and Suśruta saṃhitās) and Sato (2015) p.17 (crystal sugar ‘sometime after the first century’). See sugar-300bc-600ad::te1 and ::x2.

entries.label: Nearchus: reeds that yield honey though there are no bees
entries.hint: Nearchus, admiral of Alexander’s fleet on its voyage from the Indus to the Euphrates, reports that in India reeds yield honey although there are no bees, and that there is a tree from whose fruit honey is made, which intoxicates when eaten fresh. Preserved in Strabo, it is the first Greek description of cane juice, though it does not name the plant or a sugar.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translation read; Greek edition cited): Strabo, Geography 15.1.20, Hamilton & Falconer translation (1903), read on Perseus, whose footnote glosses the reeds as ‘the sugar-cane’; Greek ed. Radt (2005) p.160 lines 6–24 as cited by Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.20 (‘the first description of cane sugar based on an earlier, now lost, Hellenistic account, without naming it’). Translators differ on the intoxicating drink: older versions quoted by Mintz and Buttery have it made from the reed, Hamilton & Falconer attach it to the fresh fruit of the honey-tree — the Greek needs checking. Date 325 BC (Needham p.129; Ouerfelli p.18); Mintz gives 327. Dalby (2003) p.314 attributes part of the passage to Eratosthenes.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The date palm as the Near East’s sweet crop

entries.label: The date palm, store of wealth in Chaldean Babylonia
entries.hint: In the south of the Chaldean empire the date palm was the staple food and a store of wealth: temple land was leased for rents paid in dates, loans were reckoned in them, and the surplus moved north to feed Babylon. Honey and dates, not cane, were still the sweet things of the Near East.
entries.note: CONTEXT: sourcing is in babylon-1155bc-539bc::e4 and, for the older Gulf palm gardens, dilmun-3000bc-1200bc::ec5 (Kassite accounts tax the palm). No cane or sugar is attested in the Near East in this period.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Indian and Chinese hybrid canes and the first lump sugar

entries.label: The Indian and Chinese hybrid canes arise
entries.hint: On the mainland, New Guinea cane met wild S. spontaneum and hybrid canes arose that suited cooler lands: S. barberi, native to north India and grown in the Himalayan foothills from Bengal to the Punjab, and S. sinense in south China, thought to have arisen in Yunnan and adjacent provinces. The 2025 genomic study ties this continental-Asian centre of diversification to human movements about 3,000 years ago; the older Brandes hypothesis had S. officinarum introgressing with wild canes in India and China. The hybrids pushed commercial cane growing from about 25°N to 35°N.
entries.note: ANCHOR + CONTESTED: CIRAD press release (October 2025) on Garsmeur et al., Cell (2025) — diversification in continental Asia ‘some 3,000 years ago’ by hybridisation with S. spontaneum subgroups; Needham SCC 6.3 pp.130, 133–134 (S. sinense best guess Yunnan; S. barberi in the Himalayan foothills; Parthasarathy (1) p.146 on Bihar, Bengal and Orissa as the likely area of introgression; ‘researchers have not been able to establish clear centres of diversity’); Grivet et al. 2004 (not retrieved). Whether S. barberi and S. sinense arose independently of S. officinarum is disputed. See sugar-8000bc-1200bc::x1 for the older model.

entries.label: Guḍa: the first lump sugar
entries.hint: Amorphous lump sugar (guḍa, gula in Pali) appears about 300 BC in the expanded Vinaya, after the Pātimokkha’s syrup, and in the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra: sugarcane (ikṣu) occurs in all four main Dharmasūtras but guḍa only in Baudhāyana. On Daniels’s chronology India was ‘without a doubt’ the first cultural area to make sugar products.
entries.note: SECONDARY (texts not read): Needham SCC 6.3 pp.367–368 and n.a (Oldenberg (2) vol.1 pp.210, 226 and Horner (1) vol.4 pp.285, 308 for guḍa in the Vinaya; Bühler (1) for the Dharmasūtras, with Baudhāyana 1.5.12.5 and 14; the Baudhāyana ‘indicates a later date than the generally accepted time scale of −600 to −200 for sutra literature’); Mazumdar (1998) n.63 (gula, Pali for guḍa; the Vinaya Piṭaka dated to the 3rd century BC by S. N. Sen). The Arthaśāstra ladder that follows is in sugar-300bc-600ad::te1.

entries.label: Darius I annexes the Indus valley
entries.hint: Darius I made the Indus valley a Persian satrapy and sent Scylax of Caryanda down the river to Egypt, the first sustained political link between the Near East and the Indian cane country. Popular histories add that the Persians met Indian sugar here but took no real interest and mention it again only a thousand years later.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (popular claim): Buttery, A Dark History of Sugar (2022) p.8 and n.31–32, citing Macinnis, Bittersweet (2002) p.2 and Aykroyd (1967) p.13 — no primary source. The satrapy and Scylax’s voyage are standard background; see achaemenid-550bc-330bc::t3.

entries.label: Alexander’s army reaches the Indus
entries.hint: Alexander marches into the Punjab, turns back at the Hyphasis and sends his admiral Nearchus down the Indus to the Gulf: the Greeks’ first direct sight of India. Among the reports their officers bring home is the reed that yields honey without bees — the beginning of the Greek and Roman tradition of reed honey.
entries.note: BACKGROUND (standard history; the sugar link is Strabo 15.1.20 via Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) §1.1 and n.20, who says the Greeks first met cane juice during Alexander’s Indian campaign). Popular books add that samples went to Macedonia and that Alexander planted cane in Egypt; Buttery (2022) p.8 calls the latter apocryphal. See achaemenid-550bc-330bc::c8.
